<explanation>
Below is a step‐by‐step guide tailored for the OAF (Open App Filter) project – a parental control plug-in based on OpenWrt – on how to create an accurate system design diagram that reflects its architecture:

1. Identify the Project Type and Purpose:
   • The README clearly states that OAF is a parental control plug-in for OpenWrt routers, focusing on filtering apps (games, videos, chats, downloads, etc.) and allowing custom app rules.
   • The project comprises several components: a LuCI-based web interface (for configuration) and underlying filtering modules (in C) that interact with the OpenWrt kernel/system.

2. Analyze the File Structure:
   • Notice the presence of multiple packages:
     – The “luci-app-oaf” directory contains the web interface components structured with MVC patterns:
       ▪ “luasrc/controller” – handles the routing of requests.
       ▪ “luasrc/model/cbi/appfilter” – contains configuration settings and business logic.
       ▪ “luasrc/view” – includes the front-end templates (HTML) to render configuration pages.
       ▪ “htdocs/luci-static” – holds static assets such as icons and other resources.
     – The “oaf” and “open-app-filter” directories contain C source files and Makefiles:
       ▪ They implement the core filtering logic, configuration handling, possibly netlink communications with the kernel, and utilities (like JSON parsing via cJSON, regex handling, etc.).
     – The “root” folder under “luci-app-oaf” includes UCI default configuration files which integrate the plug-in with OpenWrt’s system initialization.
   • The separation into luci-app (UI) and C source code (core service/daemon) indicates a clear division between the presentation layer and the backend filtering functionality.

3. Examine the README for Additional Insights:
   • The README lays out the preparation, compilation, and installation steps. This highlights dependencies on the OpenWrt environment and the modular nature of the plug-in.
   • It shows that proper version matching with OpenWrt and kernel compatibility is essential, implying a tight integration with the router’s firmware system.

4. Creating the System Design Diagram:
   a. Identify the Main Components:
      • LuCI Web Interface Module:
        - Controller, Model, and View layers found in “luci-app-oaf” facilitate user interactions and configurations.
      • Core Filtering Service:
        - C source modules (e.g., af_client, app_filter, and others in “oaf/src” and “open-app-filter/src”) implement the actual filtering logic.
      • System Integration & Configuration:
        - UCI defaults and Makefiles that integrate the plug-in into the OpenWrt environment.
      • External Dependencies:
        - Libraries such as cJSON and regexp, plus any netlink or kernel interaction components.
   
   b. Determine Relationships and Interactions:
      • The LuCI interface (web frontend) sends configuration data via its controllers (Lua scripts) to the underlying service.
      • The service layer (C components) processes these configurations, applies filtering rules, and interacts with the OpenWrt kernel or system (likely via netlink or system calls).
      • Configuration files (such as those in “open-app-filter/files” and “luci-app-oaf/root/etc/uci-defaults”) ensure that when the router boots, the correct filtering rules and parameters are loaded.
      • Arrows in the diagram should depict data flow from user interactions (via the web interface) to the configuration service and down to the kernel-level processing.

   c. Highlight Architectural Patterns & Design Principles:
      • Use of the MVC pattern within the LuCI module for clear separation between UI and application logic.
      • Modular design that separates user interface, business logic, and system integration.
      • Clear delineation of compile-time configuration (Makefiles, UCI defaults) which enable integration into the OpenWrt system.
   
   d. List Relevant Technologies/Frameworks:
      • OpenWrt and its SDK/build system.
      • LuCI framework for the web interface.
      • C programming for the filtering engine and related network/process management.
      • Utility libraries such as cJSON and regular expression handling libraries.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   • Because this is a plug-in for an embedded system:
        - Emphasize the separation between the user-facing configuration (LuCI) and the backend filtering logic.
        - Include a clear indication of how the plug-in integrates into the OpenWrt system (bootstrapping, UCI defaults, etc.).
        - Identify interfaces between the controller (web UI) and the C-based filtering engine.
   • Use color-coding or distinct shapes to separate:
        - Web-related components (green boxes for controllers, models, views),
        - Core services (blue boxes for C modules),
        - System/integration components (yellow boxes for UCI/defaults and build configuration).

6. Instructions for Diagram Elements:
   • Add clear labels for each component like “LuCI Controller”, “App Filtering Engine”, “UCI Defaults/Configuration”, etc.
   • Use directional arrows to illustrate data flows:
        - For instance, draw arrows from “User (Browser)” → “LuCI Web Interface” → “C Filtering Daemon/Service” → “Kernel/System”.
   • Utilize color coding or varied shapes (e.g., rectangles for modules, cylinders for databases/config files, arrows for communication channels) to visually distinguish different areas and interactions.
   • Make sure each arrow includes a small note if necessary (e.g., “configuration update”, “filter rule push”, “status response”).

7. Final Emphasis:
   • Ensure the diagram is detailed and reflects every critical architectural element. Don’t hesitate to break the system into as many components as possible, as this granular view will aid in understanding each module's role.
   • Since this is architecture for an openwrt plug-in, focus on capturing the integration points with the system (like boot configuration and kernel module interfaces) as well as the clear division between the web configuration interface and the backend filtering logic.
   • Keep the diagram as clear as possible for stakeholders, with clear labels, directional data flows, and distinct sections.

By following these guidelines, you’ll be able to draft a system design diagram that accurately reflects the detailed architecture of OAF – specifically highlighting the multi-layered structure that separates the LuCI web interface from the core app filtering engine, all within the context of an OpenWrt-based system.
</explanation>
